title: Self Time per Function
statement:
A single-threaded program runs n functions with ids 0 to n − 1. Functions can call each other, and themselves. A profiler wrote a log of every call, in time order. Each entry is a string "id:start:t" or "id:end:t".

Time comes in whole units. "id:start:t" means the call begins at the beginning of unit t; "id:end:t" means it finishes at the end of unit t. So a call that starts and ends at t runs for 1 unit.

A function's self time is the number of units in which it was the one actually running, not waiting for a function it called. Return an array where entry i is the total self time of function i over all its calls. This is what the "self" column in a browser's performance profiler shows.

The log is valid: calls are properly nested, every start has a matching end, and timestamps never decrease.

examples.why: Function 1 runs units 3, 4 and 5. Function 0 spans units 0 to 8, which is 9 units, minus the 3 spent inside function 1.
A recursive call. The inner call's units still belong to function 0, so it gets all units 0 to 4.
Start and end at the same timestamp is one unit, not zero: the end is inclusive.

constraints: Each function has at least one call
hints: At any moment only one function is running: the most recent call that has not ended yet. Which data structure tracks that?
Keep a stack of open calls and a variable prev: the first unit that has not been credited to anyone yet.
On a start at t, credit t − prev to the function on top of the stack (if any), push, and set prev = t. On an end at t, credit t − prev + 1 to the popped function and set prev = t + 1.

explain.intuition:
Single-threaded means exactly one function runs at a time, and it is always the innermost open call: the one on top of a call stack. So replay the log with a stack, and between two consecutive events give all the elapsed units to whoever is on top.

The only subtle part is the unit boundaries. A start at t begins at the start of unit t, an end at t finishes after unit t. Keep prev, the first unit not yet credited. A start at t gives units prev..t−1 (that is t − prev) to the old top. An end at t gives units prev..t (that is t − prev + 1) to the function that ends, and the next free unit is t + 1.
steps: Create res of n zeros, an empty stack, and prev = 0.
Start: if the stack is not empty, add t − prev to the top's total. Push id and set prev = t.
End: pop, add t − prev + 1 to that id, and set prev = t + 1.
pitfalls: Treating the end as exclusive. Then a start and end at the same t counts as 0 units instead of 1.
Setting prev = t after an end instead of t + 1. Unit t then gets counted twice.
Subtracting the whole duration of a call from its caller even when the caller is the same function. Easier and safer: credit units as they pass, as the stack does.

complexity.space: O(L) for the stack in the worst case

solutions.title: Walk every time unit
solutions.idea: Replay the log one unit at a time: open calls that start in this unit, credit the unit to the innermost call, then close calls that end in it.
solutions.time: O(L + T) where T is the last timestamp

solutions.title: Call stack with a running cursor
solutions.idea: Only the top of the stack is running. Between events, credit the elapsed units to it; prev marks the first uncredited unit.

followups: Also report each function's total time, including the time of everything it called. What do you store on the stack?
The program has several threads and each log line carries a thread id. What changes?
